1 Introduction
Among the 3D scene reconstruction methods, active reconstruction techniques perform
poorly the application of outdoor scenes due to their high equipment cost, slow detection
speed, and poor algorithm generalization (Zhou et al. 2024a). For example, the structured
light method can perform 3D reconstruction with high accuracy, but it is not applicable
to outdoor scenes and is often used in industrial inspection and cultural relic restoration
(Zheng et al. 2020). To tackle this, with the fast acquisition speed, high equipment effi-
ciency, and high flexibility and robustness of the overall system, the passive reconstruc-
tion technique, which focuses on the multi-view stereo vision method (Li et al. 2019), has
become a popular research area with critical complexity in outdoor 3D scene reconstruction
technology. The core idea of the traditional multi-view stereo vision method is to constrain
and optimize the feature points and parameters through geometric principles. Then, the
multi-view stereo vision method can accurately recover the three-dimensional structure of
the scene from multiple two-dimensional images. The radiation field method emerged with
the development of deep learning to address the shortcomings of the traditional methods,
such as feature matching and low reconstruction accuracy, and it has shown high perfor -
mance (Yan et al. 2021). Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) (Mildenhall et al. 2020a), which is
a representative of the implicit radiation field in computer vision, is favored by researchers
for its highly realistic rendering quality, accessible and flexible scene representation, and
end-to-end learning framework. Nonetheless, NeRF models require a large amount of com-
putational resources during training and have a slow rendering speed, which makes them
difficult to integrate into in-vehicle systems to fulfill the real-time reliability requirements
of high-level autonomous driving (Zhu et al. 2023a). 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D GS) (Kerbl
et al. 2023) combines the data storage advantage of the explicit radiation field and network
optimization characteristics of the implicit radiation field to achieve high-speed operation,
high-quality rendering, and high-reliability interactions. 3D GS refreshes the SOTA of vari-
ous indicators of the 3D scene reconstruction and expects to provide strong technical sup -
port to realize high-level autonomous driving.
In terms of the rendering method, 3D GS abandons the ray tracing method represented
by NeRF and uses the fast micronizable rasterization method of a Graphics Processing Unit
(GPU) for rendering, which significantly accelerates the training process and can render in
real time. 3D GS uses ellipsoid primitives to explicitly represent the entire “body data”. And
3D GS is isomorphic to an ellipsoid, which can be obtained by deflating and rotating the
ball axially. Compared with other geometrical shapes (e.g., rectangle), ellipsoid has conti-
nuity and microscopicity, thus being able to adapt to the irregular distribution of the point
cloud, in addition to having better interpretability, computational efficiency, and robustness.
Thus, 3D GS selects the ellipsoid representation as a tiny microscopic space to flexibly and
efficiently characterize the data distribution of a realistic 3D scene. Subsequently, 3D GS
constructs the point cloud with a covariance while determining the central axis and size of
the ellipsoid by analyzing the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. 3D
GS can be sampled to obtain a similar Gaussian collection to the original data distribution.
For the rasterization of the ellipsoid, it is necessary for the researcher to implement it in
CUDA, where the process of projecting the ellipsoid onto the projection plane to get a 2D
figure is called “Splatting”. In optimizing the Gaussian body, 3D GS densifies the Gaussian
body parameters (e.g. 3D coordinates, transparency, anisotropic covariance, and spherical

Figure 1 shows the relationship between autonomous driving and 3D reconstruction
technology. Autonomous driving requires 3D reconstruction technology to help vehicles
better understand surroundings (e.g. driving scenario understanding, simultaneous localiza-

structs the environment around the vehicle, providing more accurate information about the
environment for the autonomous driving system. This helps autonomous driving systems to
better plan driving paths, avoid collisions, and improve driving safety. The emerging 3D GS
technique is an efficient 3D reconstruction method that works by mapping point cloud data
from the surrounding environment onto a 3D grid, using a Gaussian distribution function
to represent the position and size of each point. This method can represent the 3D informa-
tion of the surrounding environment more accurately and improve the sensing ability of the
autonomous driving system, enabling it to detect and recognize the surrounding obstacles
more accurately. In addition, 3D GS can effectively deal with the sparsity and noise prob-
lems of the point cloud data and improve the stability and reliability of the reconstruction
results.
Current literature has focused on 3D GS but much less in autonomous driving appli-
cation, which need explore its underlying advancements and applications in autonomous
driving. To popularize and promote the 3D GS-based scene reconstruction technology in
autonomous driving, this paper compiles the relevant subject materials of 3D GS. The
excellent overall performance and vigorous development trend of 3D GS are explored along
with the development of the 3D GS-based scene reconstruction technology, its application,
current challenges, and research frontiers in autonomous driving. Figure 2 shows that the

2 Background
2.1 3D Scene reconstruction methods
3D scene reconstruction for autonomous driving involves using sensor data to create a 3D
model or description of the vehicle’s surroundings. The purpose of this step is to provide a
real-time, accurate understanding of the environment for the autonomous driving system,
which will facilitate autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, decision planning, and
other driving-related safe tasks. 3D scene reconstruction methods can be categorized into
active and passive reconstruction techniques based on how the device collects data.
Compared with active reconstruction methods, passive reconstruction methods can
obtain image data based on natural scene illumination and solve the three-dimensional spa-
tial information of objects through specific algorithms. Because of its advantages of low
equipment cost, fast deployment, and high robustness of algorithms, passive reconstruc -
tion methods are widely used in outdoor scene reconstruction. Representative methods for
automatic driving are Monocular Stereo Vision (MSV) (Jiang et al. 2022), Binocular Stereo
Vision (BSV) (Zhai et al. 2020), and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) (Wang et al. 2021a). MSV
can reconstruct a 3D scene by using only one camera device to take photos, and its represen-
tative algorithms are Shape from Shading (SFS) (Bao et al. 2023), Shape from Texture (SFT)
(Lobay and Forsyth 2006), and Shape from Silhouettes/Contours (SFS/SFC) (Phothong et
al. 2018; Fan et al. 2022). Since conventional monocular vision systems cannot directly
measure the depth, they must rely on visual cues and a priori knowledge to estimate the
depth, which increases the complexity of the algorithm and reduces the accuracy and real-
time performance of the system. With the popularity of consumer-grade RGB-D cameras
(e.g., Microsoft’s Kinect series, Intel’s RealSense D400 series, Orbbec’s Astra series), sev-
eral studies have been conducted to reconstruct a scene in 3D based on directly acquired 3D
coordinate information. The representative algorithms are Dynamic Fusion (Newcombe et

system by generating a parallax in the design of the camera mounting position, then obtain-
ing the depth information of objects. The main idea behind BSV is to calibrate the internal
and external parameters of the camera, and subsequently match the features under Euclid -
ean geometry based on the idea of antipodal geometry. Then, BSV uses the principle of tri-
angulation to obtain the depth information and realize the three-dimensional reconstruction.
The traditional feature extraction algorithms are HOG (Shirpour et al. 2023), SIFT (Somaya
et al. 2018), ORB (Song et al. 2018), and LBP (Wang et al. 2022). With the explosion of
the extended-depth CNN model AlexNet (Nebauer 1998) in 2012, deep learning methods
have been making significant breakthroughs in 3D reconstruction and attracting the atten-
tion of researchers worldwide. To be concrete, binocular depth estimation algorithms based
on deep learning mainly include GC Net (Kendall et al. 2017), PSMNet (Chang and Chen
2018), and StereoDRNet (Chabra et al. 2019). However, the difficulty of BSV in practical
applications lies in the feature matching stage, where the matching accuracy of the left and
right camera images significantly affects the subsequent imaging effect of the algorithm.
MVS increases the number of cameras and viewpoints based on BSV . Moreover, MVS
establishes a dense correspondence based on the association of multiple images with known
camera poses, to obtain a dense 3D point cloud on the surface of the scene objects (Furukawa
and Hernandez 2013). MVS does not depend on specific external environmental conditions.
With the advantages of high accuracy, fast acquisition, and low cost, MVS is a popular
research field and a key area of difficulty in 3D scene reconstruction. Based on different
processing methods, MVS can be classified into two categories: non-deep learning and deep
learning-based frameworks. And the main mathematical representations of the scene geom-
etry are voxels, meshes, point clouds, and depth maps (Mustafa et al. 2021). Non-deep
learning-based MVS reconstruction methods rely on the ideas of parallax and geometric
constraints to reconstruct 3D scene. Non-deep learning-based methods usually use more
mature computer vision algorithms, such as feature extraction, matching, and optimization.
Thus, non-deep learning-based methods, which can be applied in a wide range of scenes,
highly depend on texture-rich regions, perform poorly on texture-poor or repetitively tex -
tured regions, and face significant challenges in complex scenes such as those with occlu-
sions, reflections, and transparent objects. Deep learning-based methods introduce excellent
ideas from the neural network and improve the reconstruction quality, automation, and effi-
ciency. MVSNet (Yao et al. 2018) extends the depth estimation method of binocular stereo
matching with the cost volume of two images to a multi-view depth estimation and proposes
a differentiable univariate responsive transform based on the cost volume. Based on MVS-
Net, subsequent improvement works [e.g. R-MVSNet (Yao et al. 2019), Fast-MVSNet (Yu
and Gao 2020), and EPP-MVSNet (Ma et al. 2021)] have mainly improved the framework
structure, model size, and computational speed, and successfully applied depth information
to the MVS problem. Deep learning-based MVS reconstruction methods can fully consider
the ambient illumination changes, encode the scene information, and extract local features,
which significantly facilitates the 3D reconstruction of non-Lambertian surfaces and weakly
textured regions (Zhang et al. 2023b). How to further develop an end-to-end MVS system
that integrates all reconstruction steps (including depth estimation, matching, filtering, and
fusion) into a unified framework for better performance and simpler pipeline is the next key
direction of research.

NeRF technology has attracted much attention from researchers since its introduction
in 2020 (Mildenhall et al. 2020a). NeRF-based 3D scene reconstruction algorithms have
excellent multi-view consistency and continuity, do not require explicit 3D annotation, and
are adaptable and easily scalable. Therefore NeRF-based algorithms have become some of
the most essential research methods for scene reconstruction. NeRF introduces two break-
throughs in the optimization of Multilayer Perceptron (MLP): Positional Encoding (PEC)
and Hierarchical Volume Sampling (HVS). PEC helps enhance the network’s ability to
accurately characterize the high-frequency details of an image, whereas HVS significantly
improves the image rendering efficiency. As shown in Fig. 3, the scene representation pro-
cess of the benchmark NeRF consists of four main parts (Zhang et al. 2023a): input of 5D
vectors, output of the color and voxel density information, voxel rendering to synthesize
the pixel colors, and a loss function to optimize the MLP parameters. The positional cod-
ing technique can map the input 5D vectors to high frequencies and facilitate the learning
process of the neural network. The multilayer voxel sampling technique can simultaneously
optimize the coarse and fine networks to obtain more sampling points without densely sam-
pling all regions on the ray. However, the NeRF method has a computational cost and high
data demand during training and rendering. It has limited processing capability for dynamic
scenes and real-time applications, so further development and improvement are necessary
(Kim et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2023b; Yang et al. 2023a).
2.2 3D GS
Despite improvements in various aspects, NeRF mainly uses implicit coordinate-based
models to map spatial coordinates to pixel values and directly renders using body rendering
and neural networks, which are computationally demanding, take too long to render, and
are costly to train. In this context, the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D GS) (Kerbl et al. 2023)
technique emerged as a paradigm-shift approach to redefine the boundary between scene
reconstruction and rendering (Chen and Wang 2024). As shown in Fig. 4, compared with
the mainstream NeRF algorithm, 3D GS retains the advantages of high-quality scene recon-
struction and ensures real-time rendering effects at the SOTA level in a short time period.
Hence, 3D GS became an essential and prominent research methodology across the field of
3D scene reconstruction by the end of 2023.

most fundamental problems. Several researchers have noted that ellipses (for which circles
are a particular case) are among the most commonly used features for 3D position esti-

regular, linear, and irregular volume datasets, so they demonstrate great adaptability and
convenience, and have attracted extensive attention from researchers. Wang et al. ( 2005)
constructed a sputtering model based on an orientation reconstruction filter kernel to address
the problem of unclear object edges in volume rendering. Due to the shortcomings of the
traditional spherical Gaussian function in 3D scenes (particularly when object surface ori-
entation or texture information is involved), Wang et al. (2005) used a directional, continu-
ous elliptical Gaussian footprint function to compress the erroneous gradient estimation in
projection, which yielded finer details of the 3D scene.
In the process of using conic curves as basic image features for research (Long 1996), the
algorithms based on ellipses for attitude estimation, stereo construction and motion estima-
tion have proved their excellent performance. However, the prior information of the camera,
number of images, and geometrical relations constrain the application and development of
ellipsoid structures in scene reconstruction. Different researchers have proposed many dif-
ferent solutions. Mai et al. (2010) proposed a method to reconstruct 3D ellipses (including
circles) from a sequence of 2D images taken by an uncalibrated camera. The minimization
problem in the transformation was transformed into a series of minimization subproblems,
which enabled the simultaneous reconstruction of multiple 3D ellipses from multiple images
and can easily handle missing ellipses and partially occluded images. Garcia et al. (2015)
approximated the 3D point cloud data to a basic elliptic model in scene reconstruction. The
model was also rendered as a set of textured elliptical splashes using multi-texturing. The
results showed that their system dramatically improved the photorealism of the rendered
point cloud while significantly reducing the modeling size. Other articles provide specific
implications regarding mathematical mechanisms and model architecture (Ivo et al. 2020;
Anjos et al. 2018). For example, Wang et al. (2019) proposed a high-fidelity differentiable
point cloud renderer algorithm, which was called the Differentiable Surface Splatting (DSS)
method. DSS handles the gradient of the point positions and normal after reasonable set -
tings. In addition, it is beneficial to enhance the ability of DSS by handles the discontinui-
ties accurately and robustly in the rendering function, large-scale topological changes and
small-scale detail modifications without explicit connections.

3 Mathematical mechanism
The interpretability of 3D GS lies in its explicit structural expression and data storage capa-
bility. An explanation of the mathematical mechanism, i.e., the working principle, of 3D GS
can help researchers analyze the complex relationships in 3D scene reconstruction technol-
ogy and reveal the performance characteristics of 3D GS in depth. In this chapter, we will
start from the main modules of 3D GS to introduce the overall computing process of 3D GS
and focus on the mathematical derivation of the core formula.
3.1 Main modules
A significant difference between NeRF and 3D GS is the explicit and implicit represen-
tations of the radiation field. The radiation field is a model that quantifies the intensity,
distribution, effect, and other parameters of light in three-dimensional space and can be

Explicit radial field representations such as voxels and point clouds should be used for

the scene, provide accurate geometric information, and facilitate multi-scale scene repre -

representation strategy to reconstruct a 3D scene using 3D Gaussian and reasonably opti-
mizes the network characteristics of NeRF by combining the series parameters. This fusion
of explicit and implicit scene reconstruction models takes advantage of the query-able and
editable nature of explicitly stored data while absorbing the automaticity and accuracy of
implicitly matched optimized data, ensuring efficient shape representation, and high-quality
rendering capability, and providing fast training speed and real-time performance.

The original 3D GS model based on three main modules: 3D Gaussian representation,
attribute optimization, and real-time rendering. Figure 5 shows its main flowchart. In the 3D
Gaussian representation module, the camera used in 3D GS is calibrated by the Structure
from Motion (SfM), and high-quality results can be obtained by only inputting the SfM
sparse point cloud when initializing the 3D Gaussians set. This strategy follows the NeRF
input strategy but outperforms most point-based solutions that require MVS data. 3D GS
also performs well on randomly initialized NeRF synthetic datasets. The superiority is that
3D Gaussian as volumetric representations can be micro-supplied for smooth rendering and
projected into a 2D space for efficient rasterization using α-blending (alpha-blending). In
the attribute optimization module, various attributes of 3D Gaussian (including the Gauss-
ian body mean and covariance in the world coordinate system, ellipsoid position, shape,
opacity, rotation matrix, magnitude, anisotropic covariance, and spherical harmonic (SH)
coefficients) must be tuned and optimized to acceptably control the behavior of the Gauss-
ian function. In practice, optimization strategies such as gradient descent, backpropagation,
and regularization, can be used in conjunction with an adaptive density control step to add,
replace, and remove 3D Gaussian. In the real-time rendering module, 3D GS draws on
tile-based rasterization research (Christoph and Michael 2021) to achieve fast GPU sort-
ing. 3D GS divides the spatial 3D scene into a series of tiny tiles. Then, each tile performs
the local sorting of the Gaussian function, utilizes the parallel processing capability of the
GPU to simultaneously perform reasonable global sorting of the data in multiple tiles, and
optimizes the memory access pattern to reduce the use of memory bandwidth to improve
the sorting efficiency. Meanwhile, the Anisotropic Splatting technique of 3D GS to ren-
der the 3D Gaussian function considers the surface orientation and texture of the Gaussian
body, so it can produce a more realistic effect in the rendering process. 3D GS uses sorting
and α-blending to normalize the order of visibility of the Gaussian and track the required
traversal of the sorted splats to significantly reduce the backpropagation time-consuming.
Thus, it achieves real-time rendering in SOTA quality at high resolution. Above all, 3D GS
successfully solves the trade-off between speed and quality of existing algorithms in the 3D
reconstruction domain by tightly integrating three key modules. The 3D Gaussian represen-

The differentiable 3D GS method has the properties of differentiable volume representation,
which can back-propagate the gradient of the rendering results to achieve gradient-based
optimization. Instead of dividing the 3D space into regular grids as in the traditional struc -

positions. By sampling the Gaussian distributions of the points in the 3D space, and cal-

clarified, so fast hybrid rendering is achieved. 3D GS can explicitly render the color and
density, which enables fast hybrid rendering. Based on the above properties, differentiable

sparse point sets and can be used as an efficient scene representation for 3D scene recon-
struction. The mathematical derivation part of 3D GS consists of three parts: representa-
tion of multivariate Gaussian functions, initialization of Gaussian bodies, and splatting of
Gaussian bodies (Kerbl et al. 2023; Zwicker et al. 2001, 2002b).

However, this literature covers a wide range and does not target autonomous driving. This
section introduces the application aspects of 3D GS-based 3D scene reconstruction technol-
ogy in autonomous driving, which contains three main aspects: new perspective synthesis,
scene understanding, and SLAM.
4.1 New perspective synthesis
Autonomous driving systems collect data from multiple sensors, which are often from dif -
ferent viewpoints and angles. A technique to fuse the data from multiple sources to create a
unified representation of the 3D scene and provide new viewpoint information is required to
help the autonomous driving system more accurately perceive and understand the surround-
ing environment. The new perspective synthesis technique converts a 3D scene to a new
perspective using 3D reconstruction algorithms (e.g., surface reconstruction and body map-
ping) to create a 3D model of the surrounding environment and convert it to a new perspec-
tive. In autonomous driving, the commonly used methods to synthesize new perspectives
are Bird’s-Eye View (BEV)-based methods (Li et al. 2023a; Cai et al. 2023), Transformer-
based methods (Wang et al. 2021b; Suhail et al. 2022), and NeRF-based methods (Mueller
et al. 2023; Yang et al. 2023c). However, in the practical application process, these meth-
ods have insufficient detail restoration, poor real-time performance, and high computational
resource requirements. Vehicles must accurately identify potentially dangerous targets dur-
ing driving, respond to emergencies in real time, and minimize the cost price of on-board
equipment. Thus, 3D GS has injected new vitality into the research of new perspective syn-
thesis with its efficient point cloud processing speed, robust surface reconstruction process,
real-time data processing performance, and flexible viewpoint conversion process.
When synthesizing new perspectives, the main challenge is to accurately model and ren-
der complex optical properties of reflective surfaces by considering how the reflective sur-
faces change their reflective content with the changes in viewing angle. The 3D GS model
initializes the Gaussian body from a sparse point cloud generated by the SfM and controls
the density of the Gaussian body by densification and pruning of the points, thus better cap-
turing the details of the reflective surfaces of objects in the scene. However, reflective sur-
faces produce high dynamic range lighting effects and reflect the details of the surroundings,
so the rendering algorithms must be able to handle complex interactions of light with the
surface, including reflection, refraction, and scattering. Discrete raw 3D Gaussian models
cannot accurately capture these details and cause distorted reflection effects. To address the
rendering problem of scenes with reflective surfaces, especially with discrete 3D Gaussian
models, Jiang et al. (2023) proposed a novel model called GaussianShader. As is shown in
Fig. 7, GaussianShader proposes a new standard estimation framework based on the short-
est axis direction of the 3D Gaussian model and designs a detailed loss function to maintain
consistent geometries of the normal and Gaussian sphere to achieve good progress and bal-
ance between efficiency and visual quality. Some researchers have noted that more details
of the scene geometry, surface materials, and ambient lighting in multi-view images can be
captured from unknown lighting conditions through innovative rendering approaches. Liang
et al. (2023) introduced 3D GS to inverse rendering and proposed a model GS-IR. GS-IR
combines a depth-derivative-based regularization method and a baking-based occlusion
method to enable a faster and more compact geometric reconstruction and a realistic and

4.2 Scenario understanding
The new perspective synthesis task aims to fuse the existing data to create a unified repre-
sentation of a 3D scene, so that vehicles can accurately understand the current environment.
Meanwhile, scene understanding is to analyze, interpret, and reason about the environment
information to identify and understand the basic properties, associative relationships, and
overall layout of the objects in the scene (Abdul et al. 2022). This process includes tasks
such as object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, scene classifica-
tion, and action recognition. Because 3D scene understanding is closer to the actual physi -
cal world and provides richer semantic information, its research results have a wide range
of application prospects inhuman-computer interaction. Thus, 3D scene understanding has
become one of the important research directions. As shown in Fig. 8, 3D scene understand-
ing can be divided into two categories: "3D + 2D" scene understanding and "3D + language"
scene understanding (Trabelsi et al. 2022); the major difference is in the methods of infor-
mation fusion and focus.
"3D + 2D" scene understanding combines 3D spatial information with 2D image infor -
mation to comprehensively interpret and explain the scene. This approach relies on image

alignment (Li et al. 2023b) or semantic alignment (Zhang et al. 2023d) to deeply fuse infor-
mation from LiDAR and the camera. However, the alignment process is limited by various
aspects such as sensor calibration errors, dynamic scene changes, and operational arithmetic
requirements. Due to the excellent performance of 3D GS, some researchers noted that the
fine-grained segmentation capability of the 2D segmentation base model can be refined
into 3D GS to avoid the enormous arithmetic and time cost of multiple forward propaga-
tions during the inference process of the traditional method. Cen et al. ( 2023a) organically
combined the 2D segmentation base and 3D GS models and proposed a model for use in the
millisecond 3D Gaussian with the fine-grained 3D interactive segmentation method SAGA.
The core strategy of SAGA is to extract 2D features and masks using the SAM model, train
the 3D features to be attached to the Gaussian body, and design the SAM bootstrap loss
and corresponding loss function to guide the training of the Gaussian body. Compared with
SA3D Cen et al. (2023b), SAGA can get 3D assets with higher quality in much less time. As
shown in Fig. 8a, Ye et al. (2023) extended 3D GS to reconstruct and segment open-world
scenes and proposed the Gaussian Grouping model. Gaussian Grouping uses the SAM
model to supervise the identity encoding of each Gaussian body in differentiable rendering.
The encoding can be effectively grouped into a specific scene based on object instances or
scene members, which demonstrates the flexibility and efficiency in scene understanding
tasks. Lin et al. ( 2024) proposed VastGaussian as a 3D GS-based method for high-quality
reconstruction and real-time rendering of large scenes through group partitioning. Vast -
Gaussian uses an incremental data partitioning strategy to achieve parallel optimization and
seamless system merging. In addition, it uses a detachable and decoupled appearance mod-
eling module to inhibit the dynamic floating of the model. As shown in Fig. 8b, Zhou et al.
(2024b) proposed a novel 3D GS-based model called HUGS based on only RGB images for

generates an exposure affine matrix by mapping the extrinsic parameters of the camera to
an exposure affine matrix, which only relies on a pre-trained recognition model (containing
noisy 2D semantic and instance predictions, noisy 2D optical flow, and noisy 3D tracking
results) to achieve the pure RGB holistic scene understanding.

understand the scene in depth by transforming the information in 3D space into natural

descriptions. Current mainstream solutions are based on methods such as Transformer (Zhu

4.3 Simultaneous localization and mapping
SLAM (Hugh et al. 1996) refers to the simultaneous localization and map building, which
aims to achieve autonomous localization and map building for intelligent systems such as
robots or unmanned vehicles by fusing the sensor data and motion models. VSLAM (Visual
SLAM) (Yan et al. 2022) relies on visual information for attitude estimation and map gen-
eration. VSLAM has outstanding advantages such as low cost, rich information, and easy
integration and is one of the key research directions in SLAM research. The NeRF-based
SLAM method uses neural networks to represent the scene radiation field, directly learns the
continuous density function in 3D space from the original pixel values, and generates a new
perspective through volume rendering techniques (Daniil et al. 2023). Compared with the
traditional single-point substitution methods, the NeRF-based SLAM has no manual feature
extraction process. It can use a gradient descent to optimize the representation of the scene.
However, it has a slower rendering speed, a low localization accuracy, and higher overall
noise in practical applications. The 3D GS-based SLAM method continues the advantages
of the NeRF-based SLAM method. Meanwhile, it is more efficient in terms of real-time
processing, localization accuracy, rendering speed, and result quality to comprehensively
improve the performance (Seongbo et al. 2024).
Yan et al. (2023) proposed GS-SLAM, which was the first model to use 3D GS repre-
sentation in the SLAM domain. GS-SLAM uses a real-time microscopic splatting rendering
pipeline to provide significant speedup ratios for map optimization and RGB-D redraw-
ing. GS-SLAM uses an adaptive scaling strategy to improve the build quality and obtains
a surprisingly fast rendering speedup in the Improvements in rendering speed. However,
regarding the overall framework operation efficiency and localization accuracy, GS-SLAM
has not significantly improved. Keetha et al. (2023) proposed SplaTAM, which was a dense
RGB-D SLAM solution based on 3D GS. SplaTAM streamlines the architecture of the
underlying 3D GS using only view-independent colors and making the Gaussian distribu-
tion isotropic. Simultaneously, it uses microscopic rendering to directly compute the gradi-
ents of Gaussian bodies and camera parameters. The final model achieves fast rendering at

Although 3D GS-based scene reconstruction techniques have achieved significant success

and high-quality features, there is still much room for improvement. For example, 3D GS

any algorithm. Although 3D GS techniques can effectively separate ground points from

When the in-vehicle system can perform a realistic physical simulation of the world

The physical simulation of the world environment can significantly enhance the safety and

shifts in the surrounding environment, and the moving intentions of dynamic targets. Xie

In vehicle navigation, accurately obtaining the spatio-temporal alignment from multi -

artificial markers and have poor generalization ability, so a reliable and trustworthy target-
less calibration method is critical in vehicle calibration. Quentin et al. (2024) proposed a 3D
GS-based calibration method, 3DGS-Calib, which has faster calibration speed and higher
calibration accuracy than the existing implicit neural methods and can efficiently complete
the in-vehicle multimodal spatio-temporal calibration task.
Currently, the more mature visual navigation technology research focuses on map repre-
sentation methods represented by Bird’s Eye View (BEV) and Occupancy Network, which
can provide more detailed environment modeling and more accurate environment under -
standing. However, BEV 2D maps are insufficient to characterize the complex textures and
detailed features of a scene, and the Occupancy Network model places severe requirements
on the arithmetic platform of the vehicle system. Thus, exploring an applicable, simple,
and efficient algorithmic framework for target navigation is one of the common goals of
researchers in automated navigation. The proposed framework enables the agent to not only
memorize the geometry and semantic information of the scene, but also retain the textural

enabled the direct mapping of spatial coordinates to color and density. The success of NeRF hinged on its ability

any burgeoning technology, it came at a cost: i) Computational Intensity. NeRF based methods are computationally
intensive [64, 181], often requiring substantial training times and resources for rendering, especially for high-resolution
outputs. ii) Editability. Manipulating scenes represented implicitly is challenging, since direct modifications to the
neural network’s weights are not intuitively related to changes in geometric or appearance properties of the scene.
It is in this context that 3D Gaussian splatting (GS) [ 111] emerges, not merely as an incremental improvement
but as a paradigm-shifting approach that redefines the boundaries of scene representation and rendering. While
NeRF excelled in creating photorealistic images, the need for faster, more efficient rendering methods was becoming
increasingly apparent, especially for applications (e.g., virtual reality and autonomous driving) that are highly sensitive
to latency. 3D GS addressed this need by introducing an advanced, explicit scene representation that models a scene
using millions of learnable 3D Gaussians in space. Unlike the implicit, coordinate-based models [ 174, 228], 3D GS
employs an explicit representation and highly parallelized workflows, facilitating more efficient computation and
rendering. The innovation of 3D GS lies in its unique blend of the benefits of differentiable pipelines and point-
based rendering techniques [197, 210, 297, 349]. By representing scenes with learnable 3D Gaussians, it preserves the
strong fitting capability of continuous volumetric radiance fields, essential for high-quality image synthesis, while
simultaneously avoiding the computational overhead associated with NeRF based methods ( e.g., computationally
expensive ray-marching, and unnecessary calculations in empty space).
The introduction of 3D GS is not just a technical advancement; it represents a fundamental shift in how we approach
scene representation and rendering in computer vision and graphics. By enabling real-time rendering capabilities
without compromising on visual quality, 3D GS opens up a plethora of possibilities for applications ranging from virtual
reality and augmented reality to real-time cinematic rendering and beyond [4, 103, 107, 192]. This technology holds
the promise of not only enhancing existing applications but also enabling new ones that were previously unfeasible
due to computational constraints. Furthermore, 3D GS’s explicit scene representation offers unprecedented flexibility
to control the objects and scene dynamics, a crucial factor in complex scenarios involving intricate geometries and
varying lighting conditions [160, 214, 320]. This level of editability, combined with the efficiency of the training and
rendering process, positions 3D GS as a transformative force in shaping future developments in relevant fields.
In an effort to assist readers in keeping pace with the swift evolution of 3D GS, we provide the first survey on 3D GS,
which presents a systematic and timely collection of the most significant literature on the topic. Given that GS is a very
recent innovation (c.f . Fig. S1), this survey focuses in particular on its principles, and the diverse developments and
contributions that have emerged since its introduction. We systematically review the foundational period of GS, with
selected works primarily sourced from top-tier conferences. Our analysis concentrates on the initial explosion of research
following its introduction in 2023 through 2024, covering the theoretical underpinnings, landmark developments, and
early applications that shaped the field. Acknowledging the nascent yet rapidly evolving nature, this survey is inevitably
a biased view, but we strive to offer a balanced perspective that reflects both the current state and the future potential
of this field. Our aim is to encapsulate the primary research trends and serve as a valuable resource for both researchers
and practitioners eager to understand and contribute to this rapidly evolving domain. The distinctions of this paper
from existing surveys (general [11, 41, 52, 267] or domain-specific [5, 10, 75]) are evident in the following aspects:

• Tiles (Patches). To avoid the cost computation of deriving Gaussians for each pixel, 3D GS shifts the precision from
pixel-level to patch-level detail, which is inspired by tile-based rasterization [122]. Concretely, 3D GS initially divides
the image into multiple non-overlapping patches (tiles). Fig. 2b provides an illustration of tiles. Each tile comprises
16×16 pixels as suggested in [111]. 3D GS further determines which tiles intersect with these projected Gaussians.
Given that a projected Gaussian may cover several tiles, a logical method involves replicating the Gaussian, assigning
each copy an identifier (i.e., a tile ID) for the relevant tile.
• Parallel Rendering. After replication, 3D GS combines the respective tile ID with the depth value obtained from the
view transformation for each Gaussian. This results in an unsorted list of bytes where the upper bits represent the tile ID
and the lower bits signify depth. By doing so, the sorted list can be directly utilized for rendering (i.e., alpha compositing).
Fig. 2c and Fig. 2d provide the visual demonstration of such concepts. It’s worth highlighting that rendering each
tile and pixel occurs independently, making this process highly suitable for parallel computations. An additional
benefit is that each tile’s pixels can access a common shared memory and maintain an uniform read sequence
(Fig. S3), enabling parallel execution of alpha compositing with increased efficiency. In the official implementation
of the original paper [111], the framework regards the processing of tiles and pixels as analogous to the blocks and
threads, respectively, in CUDA programming architecture.
3.2 Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting
At the heart of 3D GS lies an optimization procedure devised to construct a copious collection of 3D Gaussians that
accurately captures the scene’s essence, thereby facilitating free-viewpoint rendering. On the one hand, the properties
of 3D Gaussians should be optimized via differentiable rasterization to fit the textures of a given scene. On the other
hand, the number of 3D Gaussians that can represent a given scene well is unknown in advance. We will introduce how
to optimize the properties of each Gaussian in Sec. 3.2.1 and how to adaptively control the density of the Gaussians in
Sec. 3.2.2. The two procedures are interleaved within the optimization workflow. Since there are many manually set
hyperparameters in the optimization process, we omit the notations of most hyperparameters for clarity.
3.2.1 Parameter Optimization. • Loss Function. Once the synthesis of the image is completed, the difference between
the rendered image and ground truth can be measured. All the learnable parameters are optimized by stochastic gradient
descent using theℓ1 and D-SSIM loss functions:

where𝜆∈[ 0, 1] is a weighting factor. Here,LD-SSIM is formulated as 1− SSIM, derived from the structural similarity

that enforces structural consistency, ensuring that the synthesized images preserve high-frequency details and local
luminance patterns often missed byℓ1 alone.
• Parameter Update. Most properties of a 3D Gaussian can be optimized directly through back-propagation. It is
essential to note that directly optimizing the covariance matrix 𝚺 can result in a non-positive semi-definite matrix,
which would not adhere to the physical interpretation typically associated with covariance matrices. To circumvent
this issue, 3D GS chooses to optimize a quaternion 𝒒 and a 3D vector 𝒔. Here 𝒒 and 𝒔 represent rotation and scale,
respectively. This approach allows the covariance matrix 𝚺 to be reconstructed as follows:

3.2.2 Density Control. • Initialization. 3D GS starts with the initial set of sparse points from SfM or random
initialization. Note that a good initialization is essential to convergence and reconstruction quality [34]. Afterwards,
point densification and pruning are adopted to control the density of 3D Gaussians.
• Point Densification. In the point densification phase, 3D GS adaptively increases the density of Gaussians to better
capture the details of a scene. This process focuses on areas with missing geometric features or regions where Gaussians
are too spread out. The densification procedure will be performed at regular intervals ( i.e., after a certain number
of training iterations), focusing on those Gaussians with large view-space positional gradients (i.e., above a specific
threshold). It involves either cloning small Gaussians in under-reconstructed areas or splitting large Gaussians in
over-reconstructed regions. For cloning, a copy of the Gaussian is created and moved towards the positional gradient.
For splitting, a large Gaussian is replaced with two smaller ones, reducing their scale by a specific factor. This step seeks
an optimal distribution and representation of Gaussians in 3D space, enhancing the overall quality of the reconstruction.
• Point Pruning. The point pruning stage involves the removal of superfluous or less impactful Gaussians, which can
be viewed as a regularization process. It is executed by eliminating Gaussians that are virtually transparent (with𝛼
below a specified threshold) and those that are excessively large in either world-space or view-space. In addition, to
prevent unjustified increases in Gaussian density near input cameras, the alpha value of the Gaussians is set close to
zero after a certain number of iterations. This allows for a controlled increase in the density of necessary Gaussians
while enabling the culling of redundant ones. The process not only helps in conserving computational resources but
also ensures that the Gaussians in the model remain precise and effective for the representation of the scene.
4 3D GAUSSIAN SPLATTING: DIRECTIONS
Though 3D GS has achieved impressive milestones, significant room for improvement remains, e.g., data and hardware
requirement, rendering and optimization algorithm, and applications in downstream tasks. In the subsequent sections,
we seek to elaborate on select extended versions. These are: i) 3D GS for Sparse Input (Sec. 4.1), ii) Memory-efficient
3D GS (Sec. 4.2), iii) Photorealistic 3D GS (Sec. 4.3), iv) Improved Optimization Algorithms (Sec. 4.4), v) 3D Gaussian
with More Properties (Sec. 4.5), vi) Hybrid Representation (Sec. 4.6), and vii) New Rendering Algorithm (Sec. 4.7). To
provide a synthesized overview before delving into each direction, Table S1 summarizes their key ideas, representative
works (ordered chronologically), advantages, and limitations. While we have carefully selected several key directions,
we acknowledge that it is inevitably a biased view. A more comprehensive collection is given in Github.
4.1 3D GS for Sparse Input
A notable issue of 3D GS is the emergence of artifacts in areas with insufficient observational data. This challenge is a
prevalent limitation in radiance field rendering, where sparse data often leads to inaccuracies in reconstruction. From
a practical perspective, reconstructing scenes from limited viewpoints is of significant interest, particularly for the
potential to enhance functionality with minimal input.
Existing methods can be categorized into two groups (cf. Table S2). i) Regularization based methods introduce addi-
tional constraints such as depth information to enhance the detail and global consistency [32, 133, 312, 340]. For example,
DNGaussian [133] introduced a depth-regularized scheme to address the challenge of geometry degradation. FSGS [340]

devised a Gaussian Unpooling process for initialization and also introduced depth regularization. MVSplat [32] proposed
a cost volume representation so as to provide geometry cues. Unfortunately, when dealing with a limited number of
views, or even just one, the efficacy of regularization techniques tends to diminish, which leads to ii) generalizability
based methods that use learned priors [26, 240, 241, 278]. One approach involves synthesizing additional views through
generative models, which can be seamlessly integrated into existing reconstruction pipelines [ 217]. However, this
augmentation strategy is computationally intensive and inherently bounded by the capabilities of the used generative
model. Another well-known paradigm employs feed-forward Gaussian model to directly generates the properties of a
set of 3D Gaussians. This paradigm typically requires multiple views for training but can reconstruct 3D scenes with
only one input image. For instance, PixelSplat [26] proposed to sample Gaussians from dense probability distributions.
Splatter Image [241] introduced a 2D image-to-image network that maps an input image to a 3D Gaussian per pixel.
However, as the generated pixel-aligned Gaussians are distributed nearly evenly in the space, they struggle to represent
high-frequency details and smoother regions with an appropriate number of Gaussians.
The challenge of 3DGS for sparse inputs centers on how priors are modeled, whether through depth information,
generative models, or feed-forward Gaussian models. In practice, there is a trade-off between regularization-based
methods, which rely on strong constraints and per-scene optimization (favoring geometric quality but incurring
higher computation), and generalizability-based methods, which use learned priors for fast feed-forward inference
(favoring speed and cross-scene generalization, but sometimes at the expense of geometric fidelity). We summarize
these characteristics in Table S2. Future research could explore adaptive mechanisms to control this trade-off, for
example via learned confidence measures, context-aware prior selection, or user preferences, etc. In addition, while
most current methods focus on static scenes, extending these approaches to dynamic scenarios presents an exciting
direction, particularly in handling temporal consistency and motion-induced artifacts.
4.2 Memory-efficient 3D GS
While 3D GS demonstrates remarkable capabilities, its scalability poses significant challenges, particularly when
juxtaposed with NeRF-based methods. The latter benefits from the simplicity of storing merely the parameters of
a learned MLP. This scalability issue becomes acute in the context of large-scale scene management, where the
computational and memory demands escalate substantially. Consequently, there is an urgent need to optimize memory
usage in both model training and storage. Please see the excellent surveys [5, 10] for more insights on GS compression.
Recent research has pursued two primary directions to address memory efficiency. First, several approaches focus on
reducing the number of 3D Gaussians [31, 124, 188]. These methods either employ strategic pruning of low-impact
Gaussians, such as the volume-based masking [124], or represent neighboring Gaussians using the same properties
stored within a “local anchor” obtained by clustering [160], hash-grid [31], etc. Second, researchers have developed
methods for compressing Gaussian’s properties [31, 124, 183]. For instance, Niedermayr et al. [183] compressed
color and Gaussian parameters into compact codebooks, using sensitivity measures for effective quantization and
fine-tuning. HAC [31] predicted the probability of each quantized attribute using Gaussian distributions and then devise
an adaptive quantization module. These directions are not mutually exclusive; instead, one framework might use a
hybrid approach combining multiple strategies.
While current compression techniques have achieved significant storage reduction ratios (often by factors of 10-20×),
several challenges remain. One practical challenge is deploying 3D GS on edge devices, where tight memory budgets
can limit how much of a large scene can be stored or loaded locally. The field particularly needs advances in memory
efficiency during the training phase, potentially through quantization-aware training protocols, the development of

4.3 Photorealistic 3D GS
The current rendering pipeline of 3D GS (Sec. 3.1) is straightforward and involves several drawbacks. For instance, the
simple visibility algorithm may lead to a drastic switch in the depth/blending order of Gaussians. The visual fidelity of
rendered images, including aspects such as aliasing, reflections, and artifacts, can be further optimized.
Recent research has focused on addressing three main aspects of visual quality, with aliasing being specific to 3D GS’s
rendering algorithm, while reflection and blur handling represent broader challenges in 3D reconstruction. i) Aliasing.
Due to the discrete sampling paradigm (viewing each pixel as a single point instead of an area), 3D GS is susceptible to
aliasing when dealing with varying resolutions, which leads to blurring or jagged edges. Solutions emerged at both
training and inference stages. Researchers developed training-time improvements from the sampling rate perspective
and introduced schemes such as multi-scale Gaussians [283], 2D Mip filter [303] (predecessor of Mip-NeRF [12]), and
conditioned logistic function [145]. Inference-time solutions, such as 2D scale-adaptive filtering [231], offer enhanced
fidelity that can be integrated into any existing 3D GS frameworks. ii) Challenging objects. Realistic reconstruction
of objects with complex appearance, such as reflective, transparent, highly glossy, or anisotropic surfaces, remains a
long-standing problem. 3D GS inherits these difficulties because its rasterization-based pipeline only approximates
secondary effects. Recent works therefore extend 3D GS with shading functions defined on per-Gaussian normals to
better handle reflective and specular surfaces [102], with mirror attributes and plane-mirror imaging to reconstruct
mirror geometry and reflections [171], and with anisotropic view-dependent appearance fields that more faithfully
capture specular and anisotropic components [290], as well as relightable Gaussian representation [214]. Despite these
advances, robust reconstruction of reflective and transparent objects in general scenes remains challenging. iii) Blur.
While 3D GS excels on carefully curated datasets, real-world captures often suffer from blurs such as motion blur and
defocus blur. Recent approaches explicitly incorporated blur modeling during training, employing techniques such as
coarse-to-fine kernel optimization [193] and photometric bundle adjustment [325] to address this challenge.
While the approximations made in GS (Sec. 3.1) contribute to its efficiency, they also underlie artifacts such as aliasing
and blur, and limit the accuracy of illumination estimation and the modeling of challenging objects. Most existing efforts
focus on specific failure modes (e.g., anti-aliasing, deblurring, or handling particular challenging objects) rather than
providing a universal solution. In practice, one can first diagnose which issues are present in a scene (e.g., aliasing, blur,
or reflective and transparent objects) and then apply targeted optimization strategies. For static object reconstruction in
particular, faithfully modeling challenging objects such as reflective, transparent, or highly view-dependent surfaces
remains difficult despite recent progress, and extending these capabilities to dynamic or relightable scenes further
increases the complexity. The ultimate goal is to develop more general reconstruction systems that alleviate these
limitations, either through fundamental improvements to 3D GS or through brand-new architectures.
4.4 Improved Optimization Algorithms
The optimization of 3D GS presents several challenges that affect the quality of reconstruction. These include issues with
convergence speed, visual artifacts from improper Gaussians, and the need for better regularization during optimization.
The raw optimization method (Sec. 3.2) might lead to overreconstruction in some regions while underrepresenting
others, resulting in blur and visual inconsistencies.

Three main directions stand out for improving the optimization of 3D GS. i) Additional Regularization (e.g., fre-
quency [314] and geometry [139, 160]). Geometry-aware approaches have been particularly successful, preserving scene
structure through the incorporation of local anchor points [160], depth and surface constraints [28, 304, 310], Gaussian
volumes [27], etc. ii) Optimization Procedure Enhancement [34, 247, 304]. While the original strategy of density
control (Sec. 3.2.2) has proven valuable, considerable room for improvement remains. For example, GaussianPro [34]
addresses the challenge of dense initialization in texture-less surfaces and large-scale scenes through an advanced
Gaussian densification strategy. iii) Constraint Relaxation . Reliance on external tools/algorithms can introduce
errors and cap the system’s performance potential. For instance, SfM, commonly used in the initialization process, is
error-prone and struggle with complex scenes. Recent works have begun exploring COLMAP-free [219] approaches
utilizing stream continuity [59, 229], potentially enabling learning from internet-scale unposed video datasets. This line
of work removes the dependency on pre-computed SfM by jointly optimizing camera poses and Gaussian parameters
in an offline/batch manner. Readers interested in the online counterpart of this unknown-pose problem (tracking +
mapping under real-time constraints) are referred to Sec. 5.1 on GS-based SLAM.
Though impressive, existing methods primarily concentrate on optimizing Gaussians to accurately reconstruct
scenes from scratch, neglecting a challenging yet promising solution which reconstructs scenes in a few-shot manner
through established “meta representations”. Such solution could enable adaptive meta-learning strategies that combine
scene-specific and general knowledge. See “learning physical priors from large-scale data” in Sec. 7 for further insights.
4.5 3D Gaussian with More Properties
Despite impressive, the properties of 3D Gaussian (Sec. 3.1) are designed to be used for novel-view synthesis only. By
augmenting 3D Gaussian with additional properties, such as linguistic [202, 226, 347], semantic/instance [24, 295, 332],
and spatial-temporal [292] properties, 3D GS demonstrates its considerable potential to revolutionize various domains.
Here we list several interesting applications using 3D Gaussians with specially designed properties. i) Language
Embedded Scene Representation [202, 226, 347]. Due to the high computational and memory demands of current
language-embedded scene representations, Shi et al. [226] proposed a quantization scheme that augments 3D Gaussian
with streamlined language embeddings instead of the original high-dimensional embeddings. This method also mitigated
semantic ambiguity and enhanced the precision of open-vocabulary querying by smoothing out semantic features across
different views, guided by uncertainty values.ii) Scene Understanding and Editing [24, 295, 332]. Feature 3DGS [332]
integrated 3D GS with feature field distillation from 2D foundation models. By learning a lower-dimensional feature field
and applying a lightweight convolutional decoder for upsampling, Feature 3DGS achieved faster training and rendering
speeds while enabling high-quality feature field distillation, supporting applications like semantic segmentation and
language-guided editing. iii) Spatiotemporal Modeling [148, 292] (task-centric summary and comparisons are given
in Sec. 5.2). To capture the complex spatial and temporal dynamics of 3D scenes, Yang et al . [292] conceptualized
spacetime as a unified entity and approximates the spatiotemporal volume of dynamic scenes using a collection of 4D
Gaussians. The proposed 4D Gaussian representation and corresponding rendering pipeline are capable of modeling
arbitrary rotations in space and time and allow for end-to-end training.
4.6 Hybrid Representation
Rather than augmenting 3D Gaussian with additional properties, another promising avenue of adapting to downstream
tasks is to introduce structured information (e.g., spatial MLPs and grids) tailored for specific applications.

Next we showcase various fascinating uses of 3D GS with specially devised structured information. i) Facial
Expression Modeling. Considering the challenge of creating high-fidelity 3D head avatars under sparse view conditions,
Gaussian Head Avatar [277] introduced controllable 3D Gaussians and an MLP-based deformation field. Concretely,
it captured detailed facial expressions and dynamics by optimizing neutral 3D Gaussians alongside the deformation
field, thus ensuring both detail fidelity and expression accuracy. ii) Spatiotemporal Modeling (task-centric summary
and comparisons are given in Sec. 5.2). Yang et al. [291] proposed to reconstruct dynamic scenes with deformable 3D
Gaussians. The deformable 3D Gaussians are learned in a canonical space, coupled with a deformation field (i.e., a spatial
MLP) that models the spatial-temporal dynamics. The proposed method also incorporated an annealing smoothing
training mechanism to enhance temporal smoothness without additional computational costs. iii) Style Transfer.
Saroha et al. [218] proposed GS in style, an advanced approach for real-time neural scene stylization. To maintain a
cohesive stylized appearance across multiple views without compromising on rendering speed, they used pre-trained
3D Gaussians coupled with a multi-resolution hash grid and a small MLP to produce stylized views. In a nutshell,
incorporating structured information can serve as a complementary part for adapting to tasks that are incompatible
with the sparsity and disorder of 3D Gaussians.
4.7 New Rendering Algorithm for 3D Gaussians
While the rasterization-based pipeline of 3D GS offers impressive real-time performance, it still suffers from the inherent
limitations, including inefficient handling of highly-distorted cameras (for robotics), secondary rays (for optical effects
like reflections and shadows), and stochastic ray sampling (needed in various existing pipelines). In addition, the
assumptions that Gaussians do not overlap and can be sorted accurately using only centers are often violated in
practice, leading to temporal artifacts when camera movement changes sorting order. This issue is closely related to
the long-standing problem of transparency and visibility ordering in classical rasterization, where order-independent
transparency (OIT) methods aim to reduce sorting artifacts. Weighted-blended OIT [ 169] provides a widely-used
solution that approximates transparency without explicit per-pixel sorting.
Recent works [36, 166, 176] explored ray tracing based rendering algorithms as an alternative. For instance, Gaus-
sianTracer [176] introduced a new ray tracing implementation for Gaussian primitives, and devised several accelerating
strategies according to the uneven density and interleaved nature of Gaussians. EVER [ 166] deivsed a physically
accurate, constant density ellipsoid representation that allows for the exact computation of the volume rendering
integral, rather than relying on somewhat satisfactory approximations. This advancement eliminates popping artifacts.
Thanks to the fundamental paradigm shift, several exciting possibilities might emerge, including advanced optical
effects (reflection, refraction, shadows, global illumination, etc.), support for complex camera models (highly-distorted
lenses, rolling shutter effects, etc.), physically accurate rendering with true directional appearance evaluation (vs. tile
based approximation), and more. While these capabilities currently come with additional computational costs, they
provide essential building blocks for future research in inverse rendering, physical material modeling, relighting, and
complex scene reconstruction.
4.8 Kernel Engineering
Gaussian kernel is intrinsically smooth with infinite spatial support. Consequently, representing sharp boundaries,
thin surfaces, and piecewise-planar structures can be parameter-inefficient: capturing high-frequency details requires
aggressive densification and careful regularization. Furthermore, overlapping semi-transparent splats can produce
cloudy artifacts near discontinuities due to the kernel’s low-pass nature and cross-boundary leakage.

To address these limitations, a growing body of work revisits the geometric primitive and the splatting operator.
These efforts can be broadly categorized as follows: i) Surface-aligned primitives [40, 85] constrain splatted elements
to align with local tangent planes. By utilizing planar or near-planar parameterizations alongside geometric regularizers,
this direction explicitly forces primitives to match the underlying surface geometry, thereby improving multi-view
consistency and the quality of extracted meshes. ii) Alternative distributions and shape modifications [91, 130,
152, 153, 337] alter the mathematical formulation and spatial footprint of the kernel to handle sharp transitions. By
replacing the standard Gaussian with bounded-support Beta distributions, asymmetric cuts, deformable radial bases, or
heavy-tailed mixtures with subtractive components (e.g., scooping), these methods provide finer control over local
attenuation. This prevents cross-boundary density leakage and allows for a more compact representation of complex
frequency profiles and hard edges. iii) Non-Gaussian geometric primitives and operator redesigns [36, 56, 78, 294]
abandon the standard ellipsoid in favor of alternative shapes, or fundamentally modify the rendering operator (Sec. 4.7).
This includes utilizing 3D smooth convexes, trilinear point splatting into image pyramids, or bi-scale pipelines that
combine standard graphics rasterization with sorting-free splatting. These redesigns natively accommodate distinct
geometric features and bypass the limitations of pure Gaussian rasterization.
Despite rapid progress, kernel engineering introduces new practical trade-offs. Alternative parameterizations consis-
tently require custom rendering implementations and tailored primitive management strategies (e.g., modified splitting,
merging, and pruning heuristics). Furthermore, standardized evaluation remains challenging, as comparisons are
frequently confounded by differences in primitive budgets. As early hybrid pipelines begin to emerge, a promising
direction lies in the principled compression and adaptive allocation of heterogeneous primitive types – deploying
computationally complex kernels only where specific geometric intricacies demand them.
5 APPLICATION AREAS AND TASKS
Building on the rapid advancements in 3D GS, a wide range of innovative applications has emerged across multiple
domains (c.f . Fig. 3) such as robotics (Sec. 5.1), dynamic scene reconstruction and representation (Sec. 5.2), generation
and editing (Sec. 5.3), avatar (Sec. 5.4), medical systems (Sec. 5.5), large-scale scene reconstruction (Sec. 5.6), physics
(Sec. 5.7), and even other scientific disciplines [129, 266, 318, 320]. Here, we highlight key examples that underscore the
transformative impact and potential of 3D GS and offer a more comprehensive collection in Github. We also provide a
collection of representative datasets (c.f . Table S3) according to our taxonomy.
5.1 Robotics
The evolution of scene representation in robotics has been profoundly shaped by NeRF. However, NeRF’s computational
cost poses a critical bottleneck for real-time applications. The shift from implicit to explicit representation not only
accelerates optimization but also unlocks direct access to spatial and structural scene data, making 3D GS a transformative
tool for robotics. Its ability to balance high-fidelity reconstruction with computational efficiency positions 3D GS as a
cornerstone for advancing robotic perception, manipulation, and navigation in real-world environments.
The integration of GS into robotic systems has yielded advancements across three core domains. In SLAM, GS-based
methods [44, 54, 61, 62, 79, 80, 86, 97, 110, 121, 135, 168, 196, 238, 246, 279, 306, 339] excel in real-time dense mapping
but face inherent trade-offs. Visual SLAM frameworks, particularly RGB-D variants [ 110, 238, 306], leverage depth
supervision for geometric fidelity but falter in low-texture or motion-degraded environments. RGB-only approaches [86,
168, 216] circumvent depth sensors but grapple with scale ambiguity and drift. Multi-sensor fusion strategies, such
as LiDAR integration [79, 121, 262], enhance robustness in unstructured settings at the cost of calibration complexity.

properties. Multi-stage manipulation [159, 227], where environmental dynamics demand real-time map updates, requires
explicit modeling of dynamic adjustments (e.g., object motions and interactions), material compliance, etc.
The advancement of 3D GS in robotics faces three pivotal challenges. First, adaptability in dynamic and unstructured
environments remains critical: real-world scenes are rarely static, requiring systems to continuously update represen-
tations amid motion, occlusions, and sensor noise without sacrificing accuracy. Second, current semantic mapping
methods rely on costly, scene-specific optimization processes, limiting generalizability and scalability for real-world
deployment. Third, unlike NeRF based systems which can use MLP parameters as input features for downstream
decision-making, 3D Gaussians’ inherent lack of spatial order complicates feature aggregation, with no standardized
framework yet established. Bridging the gap between high-fidelity reconstruction and actionable semantic/physical
understanding will define the next frontier for 3D GS, moving beyond passive mapping towards embodied intelligence.
5.2 Dynamic Scene Reconstruction
Dynamic scene reconstruction refers to the process of capturing and representing the three-dimensional structure and
appearance of a scene that changes over time [72, 190, 191, 199]. This involves creating a digital model that accurately
reflects the geometry, motion, and visual aspects of the objects in the scene as they evolve. Dynamic scene reconstruction
is crucial in various applications, e.g., VR/AR, 3D animation, and autonomous driving [281, 331, 335].
The key to adapt 3D GS to dynamic scenes is the modeling of temporal dimension which allows for the representation
of scenes that change over time. 3D GS based methods [9, 42, 47, 73, 92, 109, 117, 127, 141, 143, 148, 162, 221, 224, 255,
263, 291, 292, 300] for dynamic scene reconstruction can generally be divided into two main categories as discussed in

(Sec. 4.6). For example, Yang et al. [291] first proposed deformable 3D Gaussians tailored for dynamic scenes. These 3D
Gaussians are learned in a canonical space and can be used to model spatial-temporal deformation with an implicit
deformation field (implemented as an MLP). GaGS [161] devised the voxelization of a set of Gaussian distributions,
followed by the use of sparse convolutions to extract geometry-aware features, which are then utilized for deformation
learning. On the other hand, the second category is based on the idea that scene changes can be encoded into the
3D Gaussian representation with a specially designed rendering process (Sec. 4.5). For instance, Luiten et al. [162]
introduced dynamic 3D Gaussians to model dynamic scenes by keeping the properties of 3D Gaussians unchanged over
time while allowing their positions and orientations to change. Yang et al. [292] designed a 4D Gaussian representation,
where additional properties are used to represent 4D rotations and spherindrical harmonics, to approximate the
spatial-temporal volume of scenes.
While 3D GS advances dynamic scene reconstruction by modeling per-Gaussian deformations, its reliance on fine-
grained primitives limits scalability and robustness. Current methods struggle to balance computational efficiency and
precision: small-scale reconstructions unify dynamic and static elements but become intractable in large environments,
often requiring manual priors to segment regions – a barrier in unstructured settings. Furthermore, the absence of
object-level motion reasoning leads to artifacts and poor generalization over long sequences. Future work might
prioritize object-centric frameworks that group Gaussians into persistent entities so as to model inherent motion
disentanglement (dynamic vs. static).
5.3 Generation and Editing
Content generation and editing are two closely related capabilities in 3D creation pipelines. Generation aims to synthesize
new assets or scenes from high-level conditions such as text and images, while editing focuses on modifying existing
content in a controlled way. In this subsection, we concentrate on works that take 3D GS as the target representation.
Please see the excellent survey [75] for more insights on the GS based generation and editing methods.
• Generation. Recent advances in GS based generation [14, 33, 53, 76, 100, 113, 125, 131, 140, 144, 149, 155, 170, 179,
186, 207, 243, 244, 269, 276, 284, 287, 289, 296, 298, 309, 313, 333, 343, 346] can be roughly grouped along the underlying
learning paradigm. Optimization-based methods follow the score-distillation paradigm: a powerful 2D or multi-view
diffusion model is queried from many camera poses, and its gradients are back-propagated through the differentiable
GS renderer to update Gaussian parameters. Early text- and image-to-3D pipelines such as DreamGaussian [244] and
GaussianDreamer [296] treat each scene independently and directly optimize positions, scales, colors, and opacities
to match diffusion-model guidance while respecting RGB reconstruction losses. This per-scene fitting often yields
high-fidelity geometry and appearance for object- and scene-level content, and can be naturally extended to dynamic
or 4D generation with temporal regularization. However, it incurs heavy computational cost (minutes to hours per
prompt) and is prone to Janus ambiguity, over-smoothing, or texture oversaturation unless additional regularizers,
multi-view diffusion priors, or geometry-aware constraints are introduced. Reconstruction-based methods decompose
the problem into two classical stages: multi-view generation followed by 3D reconstruction. Given a text or image
prompt, a pre-trained multi-view or video diffusion model first synthesizes a small set of posed views (and sometimes
depth or camera trajectories). A GS reconstructor such as LGM [243] or VividDream [125] then treats these images as
supervision and solves a standard multi-view reconstruction problem to obtain Gaussians. This design reuses mature
reconstruction pipelines and makes system-level engineering straightforward, but inherits the fundamental limitations
of the multi-view generator: imperfect cross-view consistency can lead to noisy surface geometry, duplicated structures,

the reconstruction cost and naturally promote multi-view coherence, enabling near-real-time sampling at test time.
The main challenges lie in the high-dimensional and highly structured output space (positions, anisotropic covariance,
colors, opacity), the need for large, curated 3D training corpora, and maintaining controllability (e.g., disentangling
geometry from appearance) while scaling to diverse objects and scenes. Scene-level versions further have to reason
about layout, occlusions, and long-range dependencies. Beyond applications, these methods reflect a paradigm shift
from per-scene optimization of Gaussians to amortized, feed-forward prediction (often with generative priors), enabling
much lower test-time latency and better scalability (Sec. 7).
• Editing. Current editing works [24, 29, 46, 50, 70, 83, 87, 92, 120, 158, 164, 184, 203, 221, 258, 264, 295, 300, 311, 316,

conditioned diffusion editors) to drive updates of 3D Gaussians. Representative systems such as GaussianEditor [29,
50, 184] repeatedly render GS views, apply 2D edits, and back-propagate the differences to Gaussian parameters,
enabling text- or mask-driven appearance and geometry changes. Follow-up works improve spatial localization and
multi-view consistency via attention, view correspondence, or iterative refinement [258, 264, 316], and specialize to
style transfer or personalization [311, 342]. While intuitive and compatible with powerful 2D priors, these pipelines
remain computationally heavy and can still suffer from unintended deformations due to weak 3D geometry priors.
The second family exploits the explicit, point-based nature of 3D GS for direct manipulation. Semantic or feature-
aware approaches enrich Gaussians with labels or embeddings so that users can select and edit subsets of points with
text queries, masks, or keypoints [ 24, 83, 92, 203, 295]. Mesh-coupled methods provide stronger structural control.
GaMeS [248] introduces a hybrid “Gaussian Mesh Splatting” representation where each Gaussian is parameterized by
the vertices of a mesh face; given either an input mesh or an estimated pseudo-mesh, classical mesh operations or
animations induce coherent changes in Gaussian position, scale, and orientation. GaussianMesh [63] similarly defines
Gaussians over an explicit mesh and ties the two via joint refinement: GS rendering guides adaptive face and Gaussian
splitting, while mesh constraints regularize Gaussian shapes and support large, interactive deformations driven by mesh
editing. However, this family faces several practical challenges: it relies on accurate semantic labels or mesh proxies, so
errors in segmentation or remeshing can easily produce artifacts, and editing attributes (e.g., texture, geometry, and
illumination) still requires careful regularization and cross-view alignment to preserve plausibility.
5.4 Avatar
Avatars, the digital representations of users in virtual spaces, bridge physical and digital realms, enabling immersive
interaction, identity expression, etc. Spanning entertainment (gaming, virtual influencers), enterprise (AI agents, virtual
meetings), healthcare, and education, they underpin metaverse economies. Advances in AR and VR amplify their role
in redefining social, industrial, and creative landscapes.
3D GS has emerged as a powerful tool for avatar reconstruction, primarily advancing along two directions: full-body
modeling and head-centric modeling. For full-body avatars [1, 81, 82, 94, 101, 105, 116, 126, 136, 137, 142, 177, 187,
201, 293, 305, 308, 327], the current methods typically anchor 3D Gaussians in a canonical space and deform them via
parametric body models or cage-based rigging to model dynamic motions. These approaches adopt a hybrid deformation
strategy: linear blend skinning handles rigid skeletal transformations such as joint rotations, while pose-conditioned
deformation fields account for secondary non-rigid effects like muscle jiggles. For head avatars [30, 45, 134, 200, 211,
